title: Java Read Files
learningObjectives: Read text with Files.readString and a Path.
Use BufferedReader to process a file line by line.
Handle missing files and other IOExceptions.

understand.concept: Java provides several ways to read text files. Files.readString is convenient for small files, Files.readAllLines returns all lines as a list, and BufferedReader supports line-by-line processing without loading the entire file at once. Text must be decoded using the correct character set; UTF-8 is a common explicit choice. Reading can fail, for example when a file is missing or access is denied, so handle IOException.
understand.whyItMatters: File handling allows a Java application to persist, retrieve and manage information beyond the lifetime of a single run.
understand.analogy: Think of a path as a labeled address to a storage location; the address and the data stored there are different things.
understand.analogyLimit: A path is not a guarantee that the target exists or that the program has permission to access it.

explain.narrative: Use Path.of to describe the file. For small files, call Files.readString(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8). For line collections, use Files.readAllLines. For larger files, open Files.newBufferedReader in try-with-resources and loop with readLine until it returns null. Choose the method based on file size and memory needs.

examples.explanation: readString loads the text of a small file into one String.

examples.explanation: Using the same explicit charset for writing and reading avoids platform-default ambiguity.

examples.title: Count characters
examples.explanation: String.length reports the number of UTF-16 code units in the decoded text.

practise.guidedTask: Create a small Java program that demonstrates java read files. Predict each result, then compile and run it with JDK 21.
practise.independentTask: Build a practical Java file-handling utility related to java read files. Include at least two test cases, expected outputs, and an explanation of failure handling and path safety.
hints: Start with a Path or File that points to a controlled test location.
Use try-with-resources for streams and writers, and handle IOException where the API declares it.
Test both the normal case and an edge case such as a missing path or existing target.
practise.challenge: Extend one java read files example to handle a realistic file-system edge case safely and explain the API behaviour.
